title: Love of fellow Jews
hookLine: loving other Jews whatever their practice
last: KLAL YISRAEL: ONE PEOPLE, WIDER THAN ANY STREAM.

cards: Why was the Second Temple destroyed? The Talmud asks it outright, and its answer is not about neglect. People then, it says, studied Torah.
They kept the commandments. They did acts of kindness. What had gone wrong was between them: sinat chinam, hatred for no reason, Jew against Jew.
The Talmud weighs that kind of hatred as heavy as idolatry, forbidden unions and bloodshed together. If baseless hatred can bring down a temple, the rabbis seem to ask, what holds one up?

teach.b: Ahavat Yisrael. Love of Israel, love of one's fellow Jew. Four turns.

First, the verse. Leviticus says, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." Rabbi Akiva, in a teaching kept in the early commentary called the Sifra, called this a great principle of the Torah.
Second, the verse right before it, easier to skip: "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart." Not just: don't strike him, don't cheat him. Don't keep the hatred quietly inside.
The Torah reaches into the place nobody else can see. Third, the cure. If baseless hatred tore something down, some teachers have said the repair must be its mirror image.
Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook wrote of ahavat chinam, love for no reason: love that doesn't wait for the other person to practice the way you do, vote the way you do, or deserve it first.

teach.h: THE TEST: THE JEW UNLIKE YOU.
teach.b: Fourth, the hard test. Loving Jews like you is the easy part.
Ahavat Yisrael is tested by the Jew in the other stream, whose Shabbat you would never keep, whose politics you argue with. It doesn't erase the arguments.
This week ran from the traditional middle, through no label and lay-led rooms, to shared ethics, disagreeing with love, and the whole people. Ahavat Yisrael keeps all of them in the same house.

how: Jews speak of ahavat Yisrael when they help, host or pray for Jews unlike themselves, and teachers in several streams cite the Talmud's account of baseless hatred as a warning.

o: love for the land of Israel and its places
loyalty only to Jews who practice like you
love for your fellow Jew, whatever their practice

p: a great principle of the Torah
don't hate thy brother in thine heart

s: the Talmud says the Second Temple fell because people stopped studying Torah
it says they studied, kept commandments and did kindness; the problem was baseless hatred.
the Torah forbids hating your brother even in your heart
"Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart."
ahavat Yisrael means loving only Jews who practice like you
its real test is the Jew unlike you.

games.q: a relative's way of practicing seems wrong to you, and you've been cool toward them for a long time. what does ahavat Yisrael ask?
o: wait for them to change first.
set down the quiet grudge and take one small step toward them.
avoid the subject and the person.
games.why: the verse forbids hatred kept in the heart, and Rav Kook's answer to baseless hatred was love that doesn't wait to be deserved.

practice: Find one divide in your own life: a cousin who practices differently, a neighbor across a political line, an old friend you stopped calling after an argument.
Look for anything you've been holding against them quietly, the hating in the heart the verse means, and set it down for these two minutes; you don't have to fix it.
Then picture one small step across, a message, a question, a kind word, and if you pray, hold them in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Ahavat Yisrael. Love of one's fellow Jew, whatever their practice, rooted in the verse "love thy neighbour as thyself." Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: love of Israel, love of one's fellow Jew.

carryVoice: Your line: love your fellow. Love for no reason doesn't wait to be earned. A week, complete.
